newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: INTROSPECTIVE S.AFRICAN SHARES SET FOR TOUGH WEEK.
newsitem.headline: INTROSPECTIVE S.AFRICAN SHARES SET FOR TOUGH WEEK.

text.p: South African shares will have a tough time next week shaking off the negative sentiment that has severely battered them over the last five trading sessions, dealers and economists said on Friday.
The market has steadfastly ignored all international factors and focused on its own internal problems. The introspective mood seems set to continue.
As Wall Street has continued to break record highs, the Johannesburg Stock Exchange has sank lower. At 1100 GMT the all-share index was down 10.2 points at 6,792.7.
"We are certainly concentrating on our local woes. We are not taking any hint from international markets," said Mark Appleton, fund manager at NBS.
Last month's collapse in the rand -- which has now lost some 30 percent against the U.S. dollar since mid-February -- has sparked renewed debate on the scrapping of exchange controls.
Coupled with a money market squeeze, that in turn has provoked fears of a hike in interest rates.
On Friday Reserve Bank governor Chris Stals ruled out a "big bang" approach to getting rid of the controls and said phasing them out would take four or five years.
But economists said the comments would not see the issue go away.

"The country is between a rock and a hard place in terms of wanting to do something on exchange controls, but not being able to do so," said Andre Joubert, portfolio manager at Investec Asset Management.
"As long as nothing happens the rand is going to be under pressure and so the negative sentiment is expected to prevail," he said.
Fears on the currency will again be uppermost in the minds of dealers and investors.
"The currency is the absolute concern at the moment, playing the biggest role in the direction of the market," one dealer said.

This week has seen better-then-expected data on producer price inflation and the level of October gold and foreign exchange reserves. But the share market has ignored the upside and instead concentrated on some poor company results.
First National Bank , cement firm PPC , Rainbow Chicken , Plate Glass , clothing retailer Edgars and Coke bottler ABI all posted disappointing figures.
With no major new economic data due next week the scope for recovery of a significant amount of this week's losses is limited.
Instead market eyes will be fixed on corporate earnings. On Monday Syfrets brings out year figures, followed by half year results from South African Breweries and Southern Life on Wednesday.
Analysts fear SAB may disappoint as it generates some of its earnings from its stakes in ABI, Plate Glass and Edgars.
With the market in an unforgiving mood, woe betide any company that comes in under expectations. "Where there is bad news the market is going to be particularly severe," Joubert said.

But some stocks may stand to benefit next week as investors fleeing this week's bloodshed seek out quality. "The market will also reward those companies that are seen to have positioned themselves well for the current economic climate," Joubert said.
On Tuesday the interim Platinum review from Johnson Matthey will be released in London and could influence Amplats and Implats shares.
